subject: Post-incident Q&A: log retention & forensic data handling
messages:
From: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@clientops.com>
To: marissa_cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Subject: Questions: post-incident log retention & forensics

Hi Marissa,

Thanks again for the runbook walk-through yesterday. A couple of follow-ups from our security team around what happens after an incident: specifically, how long Redwood keeps request logs and any derived forensic artifacts, and what the process is if we need to extend retention for a legal hold. We need this for our internal incident response checklist and to satisfy our legal counsel.

High-level questions:
- What are your default retention windows for request-level logs (request/response bodies, K/V cache snapshots, system traces)?
- If we ask for an extended retention (e.g., legal hold), what is the human process (who signs off) and the technical mechanism (snapshots, copy to a secure bucket, access controls)?
- How do you ensure chain-of-custody and immutable storage for forensic exports?

Could you share any short doc or pointer to the playbook? Appreciate a quick answer we can include in our report.

Best,
Alex
Senior Security Ops, ClientOps

From: marissa_cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Cc: evelyn_hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.com>, rishi_malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Questions: post-incident log retention & forensics

Hi Alex — thanks for the clear list. Looping in Evelyn (Security) and Rishi (Sales/legal touchpoint) — Evelyn will have the most accurate operational details; Im also attaching the short playbook excerpt for quick reference.

Quick answers up front:
- Default request-level logs: retained 90 days by default for hosted customers; dedicated/private customers can set retention per SLA.
- Legal hold/extension: requires a written request from an authorized contact + approval from Security and Legal. Technical step is a secure snapshot/export to an encrypted, access-restricted bucket tied to the request.
- Chain-of-custody: exported artifacts are checksummed, signed by an S3 object-level manifest, and access-tracked via audit logs.

Evelyn — can you expand on the forensics export process and the steps we follow for cross-border data considerations?

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Attachment: forensic_playbook_v2.pdf (summary section included below)

From: Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.com>

Hi Alex / Marissa,

Thanks for the ping. Below is a concise operational summary you can paste into your checklist. Happy to jump on a quick call if you want more detail.

Operational summary (post-incident forensic data handling):
1) Default retention windows
   - API request/response metadata (headers, timestamps, model id): 365 days for enterprise accounts by default; hosted (self-serve) default = 90 days.
   - Full request/response bodies (user-provided prompt text & model output): default 90 days for hosted; customer-configurable for Dedicated/Private.
   - KV cache snapshots and runtime trace artifacts: 30 days by default, unless a retention policy is configured otherwise.

2) Expansion/Legal hold process
   - Trigger: customer request from an authorized admin + internal incident ticket (SEC-487).
   - Approvals: Security + Legal + Account Owner sign-off. Rishi can assist with confirmation of authorized signatories.
   - Technical action: create a time-stamped immutable snapshot of relevant logs and artifacts, copy to a WORM-enabled encrypted bucket in the customers chosen residency region (if configured), and attach an audit manifest (SHA256 checksums + signer metadata).

3) Chain-of-custody and integrity
   - Each export receives a manifest file with SHA256 checksums and a signed statement (KeyID) from Redwood's HSM-backed KMS.
   - Export operations are logged to an append-only audit stream; access to the export is role-based with MFA required.
   - For critical incidents, we also notarize the manifest internally (internal ticket number + timestamp) and retain the notarization record for the duration of the legal hold.

4) Cross-border / residency considerations
   - By default, forensic exports are placed in the same region as the tenants primary residency. If export to another region is requested, Legal review is required and data transfer controls are applied.
   - For customers with a strict residency requirement (e.g., EU data never leaving EU), Redwood supports in-region snapshots and export to customer-managed buckets within the region.

5) Access and temporary retention extension
   - Temporary retention extensions are implemented via snapshot + retention flag; tickets include a TTL and an assigned custodian.
   - Access to retained artifacts is limited to named individuals; we require documented justification for access during reviews.

Attachments referenced: forensic_playbook_v2.pdf (sections: Export Process, Manifest Format, Custody Controls). Ive attached the short playbook excerpt to this thread.

If you need a formal statement for Procurement/Legal, Rishi — can you prepare the short approval template we normally use?

Cheers,
Evelyn Hart
Senior Security Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: David Kim <david_kim@redwood.com>

Hi Alex — quick technical clarifications from infra/forensics: 

1) Bucket ownership & keys:
   - For Hosted customers: Redwood provisions the WORM-enabled bucket in the region requested; objects are encrypted with a customer-dedicated envelope key managed in Redwood's KMS by default. If a customer provides their own KMS (BYOK) we can encrypt the exported artifact with the customers key and copy to either a Redwood-managed or a customer-managed bucket depending on contract.
   - For Dedicated/Private: default is to export into a customer-managed bucket (recommended) with BYOK; we only provision buckets into customer tenancy upon explicit written agreement.

2) Turnaround & evidence for EU-region exports:
   - Typical turnaround: 24-72 hours for a standard export (depends on dataset size). For high-priority incidents we have a fast-track procedure (target < 8 hours) once approvals are in place.
   - Validation: the export manifest includes the region and the target bucket ARN; we provide the SHA256 manifest and an S3 object metadata record, plus an audit log slice showing the copy operation with timestamps and operator identity. For EU residency constraints we also include a signed statement that the export target was in the EU region and the copy never left the region.

Operational notes: when we perform an export we create a Jira ticket (linked above) and attach the manifest + checksums. Export operations are reversible only by creating a new export and deleting the source snapshot; we keep the original snapshot immutable.

Happy to coordinate the necessary approvals if ClientOps wants to run through a dry-run.

-David
David Kim
SRE / Forensics, Redwood Inference
